title: Infrastructure: GPU Fleet, CI/CD, and IaC Guidelines
author: Aisha Khan
body:
Overview

This page consolidates the infrastructure engineering best practices and standards for GPU fleet capacity, cloud account & networking patterns, Terraform/IaC module design, and CI/CD/build pipelines used by the eng-infra team. It is intended as a canonical reference for on-call engineers, SREs, and infra contributors.

Scope

- GPU fleet sizing, autoscaling and capacity planning
- Cloud account structure, VPC design, and networking primitives
- Terraform module patterns, versioning, and registries
- CI/CD pipelines, release gating, and build artifact management
- Runbooks and operational playbooks for common failure modes

Goals and Principles

1. Predictable capacity: support target SLOs for latency and throughput with defined headroom and burst capacity for spikes.
2. Declarative, reviewable infrastructure: all production infra is managed via IaC (Terraform) and reviewed via CI.
3. Small, composable modules: modules should be reusable across accounts/regions with clear inputs and outputs.
4. Automate safety: CI gates, canary rollouts, and automatic rollback on regressions.
5. Observability and runbooks: every service must have dashboards, alerts, and an associated runbook.

GPU Fleet and Capacity

Requirements and SLOs
- Production inference SLOs: P95 latency <= 200ms for small-context requests (<= 1k tokens) and P99 latency <= 800ms for long-context workloads.
- Availability SLO: 99.95% monthly for dedicated inference pools.
- Capacity headroom: maintain minimum 20% spare capacity during business hours and 10% off-hours.

Instance types and sizing
- Preferred instance families: A100-40GB, H100-80GB, and L4 (cost-optimized) depending on model profile.
- Pod sizing guidance: use homogeneous pools per instance class. Document supported models per pool.
- KV cache memory sizing: reserve 1.2x peak KV memory for safe operation.

Autoscaling and policies
- Autoscaler: cluster-autoscaler (customized) + request-level routing to fall back pools.
- Scaling thresholds: scale-up when average GPU utilization > 70% for 2 consecutive minutes. Scale-down only after 20 minutes below 40% utilization and respecting cooldown windows.
- Burst capacity: reserved burst pool per region (configurable by workspace) to absorb sudden spikes; billing attributed via tag/labels.

Capacity planning cadence
1. Weekly: 7-day lookahead based on traffic and scheduled experiments.
2. Monthly: run load tests (see benchmarking playbook) and validate headroom.
3. Quarterly: model onboarding review to estimate new memory/throughput requirements.

Failure modes & mitigation
- Out-of-capacity: automatic routing to lower-cost model variant or upstream fallback (hosted API) with rate-limited degradation.
- Kernel OOMs: kill and restart container, escalate if repeated (>3x in 1h).
- Network packet loss: route traffic to alternative AZ/region if cross-AZ loss > 1%.

Cloud Accounts and Networking

Account Structure
- Org root: single Redwood cloud org.
- Tenancy: separate accounts per environment (platform-prod, platform-staging, infra-shared, sandbox-team-*) and customer-dedicated accounts for Private deployments.
- Account tags: team, environment, cost-center, region, project.

VPC and network design
- Hub-and-spoke: a centralized networking hub account for shared services (NAT, DNS, central logging) and spoke accounts for workloads.
- Subnet strategy: public subnets for load balancers; private subnets for inference pools; isolated subnets for management plane.
- Cross-account peering: use VPC peering or transit gateway per region. Prefer Transit Gateway for >3 peers.
- Network ACLs & Security Groups: default-deny inbound; least-privilege egress for control plane components.

Connectivity and Egress
- Egress control: use NAT gateways in the hub; restrict egress with egress-only endpoints for sensitive regions.
- Private link: host control-plane APIs via VPC endpoints where supported.
- BGP and on-prem: route via VPN/Direct Connect with redundant paths for Private deployments.

IAM & cross-account access
- Principle of least privilege. Group-based permissions and role assumption for cross-account operations.
- Short-lived credentials: prefer OIDC/STS with session durations limited to 1 hour for automation runners.

Terraform / IaC Modules and Patterns

Module design principles
- Single responsibility: each module does one logical piece (network, compute-pool, iam-roles, observability).
- Stable inputs: avoid changing input names frequently. Provide sensible defaults and required flags.
- Outputs: expose only necessary IDs and ARNs; keep outputs minimal and semantic.
- Versioning: use semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Pin module versions in environment overlays.

Registry and module publishing
- Internal registry: modules are published to our internal Terraform registry (artifactory/registry). PRs must bump version and include CHANGELOG entry.
- Module review: every module PR requires 2 approvals (IaC owner + security reviewer).

Example: compute-pool module usage
```
module "inference_pool" {
  source  = "registry.internal.redwood/infra/compute-pool"
  version = "1.3.0"

  name             = "inference-prod-a100"
  instance_type    = "nvidia-a100-40gb"
  desired_capacity = 20
  min_capacity     = 4
  max_capacity     = 120
  region           = "us-west-2"
  subnet_ids       = module.network.private_subnets
  tags = {
    team        = "eng-infra"
    environment = "prod"
  }
}
```

State management and workspaces
- Remote state: use encrypted remote state (S3 with KMS) and state locking (DynamoDB).
- Workspace per environment: prod/staging/dev workspaces. Avoid long-lived feature workspaces for infra changes; use PR previews instead.

CI/CD and Build Pipelines

Pipeline principles
- All changes go through Git (main protected). PRs are gated by plan & policy checks and automated integration tests.
- Pipeline stages: fmt -> lint -> terraform plan (in preview) -> integration tests -> terraform apply (manual approval for prod).
- Tracing & artifacts: build artifacts (AMI/container images) are immutable and stored in artifact registry with immutable tags.

Example pipeline (condensed)
```
name: infra-ci
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  fmt-lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [checkout, terraform fmt, tflint]

  plan:
    needs: fmt-lint
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [checkout, terraform init, terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan]
    outputs:
      plan-file: plan.tfplan

  policy-checks:
    needs: plan
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [opa eval policy.rego plan.tfplan]

  apply-prod:
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name == 'push'
    needs: policy-checks
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [manual approval, terraform apply plan.tfplan]
```

Secrets and credentials
- Use secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager) or HashiCorp Vault for sensitive values. CI runners fetch short-lived credentials via role assumption.

Build artifacts and container images
- Image immutability: tag images with sha256 and promotion pipeline for staging->prod.
- Scanning: image vulnerability scan on build; fail on critical vulnerabilities.

Runbooks and Operational Playbooks

Every critical infra service/pool must have a runbook with: ownership, key dashboards, common symptom checks, mitigation steps, rollback steps, and post-incident checklist. Examples included: GPU OOM, node termination, control-plane outage, cross-region failover.

Runbook excerpt: GPU out-of-capacity
1. Verify alerts: review capacity alert dashboard and recent scale events.
2. Check autoscaler status: kubectl get hpa / aws autoscaling describe-scaling-activities.
3. Failover: route traffic to fallback pool or degrade to lower-capacity model with configured policy.
4. Temporary mitigation: increase desired_capacity on compute pool by +20% in the control plane (manual) and monitor for safety.
5. Post-incident: record root cause, capacity delta, and update capacity planning spreadsheet.

Change Management and Rollouts

- Canary policy: start with 5% traffic for 30 minutes, then 25% for 60 minutes before full rollout.
- Rollback criteria: increased error rate > 1% or latency regressions exceeding thresholds for 15 minutes.
- Communication: update on-call channel and incident channel for significant rollouts.

Contribution and Team Wiki Practices

- Page templates: use the infra runbook template for operational docs and module template for Terraform modules.
- How to propose changes: open a PR in the infra-docs repo with the proposed doc and link to the related module/service.
- Documentation ownership: every module and runbook must list an owner and at least one secondary reviewer.
